title: An Overview of Open-End Spinning: Rotor, Air-Jet and Friction Spinning
description: Read article about This article explains how rotor, air-jet, and friction spinning raise yarn productivity, shape yarn structure, and serve denim, sheeting, and technical textiles. and more articles about Textile industry at Fibre2Fashion
head:
Key Takeaways
Rotor, air-jet, and friction spinning were developed to bypass ring spinning’s speed limit by separating twist insertion from package winding and working directly from sliver.
Rotor spinning has the widest use, balancing productivity, yarn quality, and count range, while producing bulkier, more abrasion-resistant yarns that are generally weaker than ring yarns.
markdown:
Ring spinning has been the dominant method of staple yarn production for over a century. It produces strong, fine yarns. Its limitation is speed. In ring spinning, twist is inserted by rotating the whole yarn package. Package rotation and traveller speed set a ceiling on output.

The new spinning systems were developed to overcome this ceiling. They separate twist insertion from package winding. Three systems are most important commercially: rotor spinning, air-jet spinning and friction spinning (Lawrence, 2003; Lord, 2003).

The Open-End Principle

In open-end spinning, sliver is opened into individual fibres, which are carried to a collecting surface and reassembled. Twist is inserted at the “open” end of the forming yarn, while the package only winds the yarn. The package therefore does not need to rotate for twist insertion, allowing higher delivery speeds and larger packages.

Rotor and friction spinning are true open-end systems; air-jet spinning is not. Air-jet spinning keeps the fibre strand continuous and uses air to wrap surface fibres around a core. It is grouped with open-end systems because it also aims to achieve high productivity from sliver in a single step (Lawrence, 2010).

Rotor Spinning

1. Principle and Mechanism

Rotor spinning is the most widely used open-end system. Sliver is fed against a fast opening roller fitted with card clothing or pins, which separates it into individual fibres. An air stream carries the fibres through a transport duct into the rotor.

The rotor is a small cup that rotates at high speed. Centrifugal force pushes the fibres into a groove on its inner wall, where they collect as a thin fibre ring. This process, called back-doubling, reduces short-term variation in fibre feed.

The yarn end lies in the groove and links with the fibre ring. Each rotor revolution inserts one turn of twist. Take-up rolls withdraw the yarn through the doffing tube (navel), and the yarn is wound onto a cross-wound package (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Rotor spinning process

2. Yarn Structure and Properties

Rotor yarn has a twisted core with loose “wrapper” or “belt” fibres on the surface. These fibres form where fibres bridge the yarn end as it leaves the groove. Rotor yarns are generally more even and regular than ring yarns and are bulkier and more abrasion-resistant. However, they are usually 10–20 per cent weaker and have a harsher handle.

3. Applications

Rotor spinning suits coarse and medium counts and is widely used for denim, towelling, bedsheets, knitted fabrics and industrial textiles. It also processes short and recycled fibres effectively.

Air-Jet Spinning

1. Principle and Mechanism

In air-jet spinning, sliver passes through a roller drafting system, often with three or four rollers and aprons. The drafted fibre strand then enters one or two air nozzles, where tangentially supplied compressed air creates a swirling vortex.

In twin-nozzle systems, the second nozzle inserts false twist into the core while the first rotates in the opposite direction and wraps edge fibres around it. When the false twist unwinds after the nozzle, the wrapper fibres tighten around the parallel core. The yarn is then delivered by rollers and wound onto a package (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Twin-nozzle air-jet spinning process

Murata’s MJS (Murata Jet Spinner) was the first major commercial system. The later vortex spinning system (MVS) uses a single nozzle with a hollow spindle and produces a higher proportion of wrapper fibres, giving a more ring-like yarn.

2. Yarn Structure and Properties

Air-jet yarn is a fasciated yarn with a core of nearly parallel, largely untwisted fibres held by wrapper fibres at intervals. It has low hairiness and good pilling resistance but is weaker than ring yarn and stiffer in handle.

3. Applications

Air-jet spinning works well with polyester, viscose and polyester-cotton blends and suits medium to fine counts. It provides the highest delivery speeds among these systems and is used for shirting, sheeting, knitwear and home textiles.

Friction Spinning

1. Principle and Mechanism

Friction spinning is an open-end system best known through the DREF machines developed by Ernst Fehrer. Sliver is opened by a carding or opening roller, and an air stream carries the fibres into the nip between two perforated drums.

The two drums rotate in the same direction, while suction through their perforations holds the fibres in the wedge-shaped nip. Friction between the rotating surfaces rolls the fibre assembly and inserts twist. The yarn is withdrawn along the drum axis, at right angles to the fibre feed (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Friction (DREF) spinning process

DREF-2 produces yarn from staple fibres alone. DREF-3 adds a drafted core strand around which fibres from the friction zone wrap, producing core-sheath yarns with improved strength.

2. Yarn Structure and Properties

Friction-spun yarn has a core-sheath structure with uneven twist from core to surface. Fibre orientation is poor, and fibres are often buckled or folded. The resulting yarn is weak and bulky and is suited to coarse counts.

3. Applications

Friction spinning has a narrow but important market. It is used for coarse yarns, blankets, upholstery and filter fabrics. Its core-spun capability supports technical applications, including heat-resistant yarns with aramid sheaths and conductive core yarns. It can also process waste and recycled fibres.

Structure of the Resultant Yarns

Each system produces a distinct yarn structure, shown in simplified form in Figure 4. Rotor yarn has a twisted core with irregular wrapper fibres; air-jet yarn has a parallel core bound by wrapper fibres at intervals; and friction-spun core yarn has a central strand covered by wrapped fibres. These structural differences influence strength, handle and hairiness.

Figure 4: Structure of (a) rotor-spun, (b) air-jet and (c) friction-spun yarns

Summary

The three systems differ in their method of twist insertion: rotor spinning uses a rotating cup, air-jet spinning uses swirling compressed air, and friction spinning uses the rolling action of two drum surfaces. Air-jet generally provides the highest delivery speed, while rotor spinning offers a balance of speed, yarn quality and count range and has the largest installed base.

All three produce structures different from ring yarn and do not fully match it in strength or softness. System selection therefore depends on end use, fibre type and count range (Lord, 2003).
